R01-F-01: Students meeting physics for the first time are often unsettled to learn that the planes in their textbooks have no friction, the pendulums swing without air, and the planets are treated as points. Economics and population biology are worse offenders: their agents calculate perfectly and their populations are infinitely large. A natural response is to say that science, at least in its models, trades truth for convenience, and that a model is a useful fiction whose only virtue is that it lets us calculate. On this view the idealisation is a debt to be repaid later, when better methods allow the missing details to be added back. This response gets the matter backwards. An idealisation is not usually a lapse in description but a claim about relevance. To leave friction out of an account of a stone sliding down a smooth slope is to assert, implicitly, that friction makes no appreciable difference to the feature one is trying to explain, namely the way the stone's speed grows with time. If that assertion is correct, the idealised model is not a fiction about the stone; it is a true statement about what the stone's motion depends on. The model is false about the world in its details and accurate about the structure of dependence, and the second is frequently what we wanted to know. Adding every missing factor would not improve such a model; it would bury the very pattern the model was built to display. This does not mean that every idealisation is innocent. The claim of irrelevance can be wrong, and it is often wrong in a particular way: an assumption that holds well within one range of conditions fails outside it. Treating air as absent is harmless for a stone dropped from a window and disastrous for a feather, or for a parachutist. The danger lies less in the falsehood itself than in forgetting that it was a bet about relevance, so that a model calibrated in one setting is carried into another where the bet no longer pays. The sensible test, then, is not whether a model is literally true, since almost none are, but whether its conclusions survive when the idealisation is relaxed. If a result about a population holds whether the population is taken to be infinite or merely very large, the assumption of infinity was doing no harm. If the result vanishes as soon as the assumption is loosened, it was an artefact of the simplification rather than a discovery about the world. Read in this way, the frictionless plane is less an embarrassment than a hypothesis, and like any hypothesis it can be checked.
R01-F-02: A long tradition in the philosophy of science treats explanation and prediction as two faces of one achievement. To explain why an event happened, on this view, is to show that it could have been expected, given the relevant laws and the conditions that held beforehand; to predict an event is to perform the same derivation before the event rather than after it. The symmetry is attractive because it makes explanation answerable to something. An explanation that could not, even in principle, have served as a prediction would seem to be no more than a story told after the fact. The view also promised a single standard for the whole of science, from astronomy, where eclipses are calculated centuries ahead, to clinical medicine, where a diagnosis is expected both to account for a patient's symptoms and to anticipate their course. Yet the symmetry fails in both directions. A falling barometer reading is an excellent predictor of a coming storm, and anyone who knows the correlation can forecast the weather with it; but no one supposes that the barometer explains the storm. Both are effects of a drop in atmospheric pressure, and the reading earns its predictive power by riding on that common cause. Conversely, we can often explain what we could never have predicted. A geologist can say why a particular hillside gave way, pointing to saturated soil and a weakened layer of clay, without having been able to say beforehand that it would fail that week rather than in some other year. The explanation is sound even though the forecast was out of reach. What these cases suggest is that explanation and prediction answer to different demands. A predictor need only be reliably connected with what it predicts; it does not matter how the connection arises. An explanation must identify what the outcome depends on: the factors such that, had they been different, the outcome would have been different too. The barometer fails that test, since a broken barometer would not have prevented the storm; the clay passes it, since firmer clay would have held the slope. None of this makes prediction irrelevant to explanation. A claim about what an outcome depends on usually implies something about what would happen under other conditions, and checking those implications is how such claims are tested. A theory that explains everything and forbids nothing should make us suspicious. But the test is a check on an explanation, not its substance. To confuse the two is to mistake the evidence that an account is right for the thing that makes it an account at all.
R01-F-03: The sceptical argument about induction, usually traced to David Hume, has a disarming simplicity. Every inference from observed cases to unobserved ones assumes that the future will resemble the past, or more generally that nature is uniform. That assumption cannot be proved by logic, since its denial involves no contradiction, and it cannot be supported by experience without circularity, since the support would itself be an inference from observed cases. Philosophers have spent a long time looking for a way out, usually by searching for a single principle that would license inductive inference in general. The search may be misconceived, because there is no such thing as inductive inference in general. Consider two investigators. One measures the melting point of a newly prepared sample of a pure compound and concludes, from a single careful trial, that every sample of that compound will melt at the same temperature. Another measures the height of one adult and draws no conclusion at all about the heights of adults. Both are reasoning well, and they differ not because one has found the universal principle and the other has not, but because each knows something about the kind of thing being studied: that pure compounds are uniform in their melting points, and that people are not uniform in their heights. On this picture, what licenses an inductive step is not a principle of uniformity but particular facts about particular domains, which tell us how far a sample can be trusted to stand in for the whole. The obvious objection is that this merely relocates the problem. Our confidence that compounds are uniform in their melting points was itself acquired by induction, and so the sceptic can ask what licenses that. The objection is fair, but it is less damaging than it looks, because it trades on an ambiguity between justifying each belief and justifying all of them together. The regress it describes is real, yet it never requires us to justify all our inductive habits at once. At any moment we lean on some background knowledge in order to test some other part of it, and any item can in turn be questioned while the rest is held fixed. This does not answer the sceptic on the sceptic's own terms, which demand a foundation lying outside experience altogether. It does show that the demand is not one that science, as actually practised, needs to meet in order to be rational, any more than a household needs to audit every account on the same afternoon in order to keep honest books.
R01-F-04: Faced with two theories that fit the evidence equally well, scientists usually prefer the simpler, and they rarely feel the need to say why. When pressed, they tend to offer one of two answers. The first is that simplicity is a convenience: simpler theories are easier to state, to teach and to calculate with, and so they deserve priority in the way that a tidy desk deserves priority over a cluttered one, without any suggestion that tidiness is truer. The second is that nature itself is simple, so that a simple theory is more likely to have captured how things are. Neither answer is satisfactory. The first explains why we might enjoy simple theories but not why we should believe them, and the second asserts, with no evidence that could be independent of the very preference in question, exactly what needed to be shown. A more promising answer comes from an unglamorous source, the practice of fitting curves to data. Any finite set of measurements, each carrying some error, can be fitted perfectly by a sufficiently complicated curve, one that bends to pass through every point. Such a curve is usually a worse guide to the next measurement than a smoother one that passes near the points without touching them all, because much of what it has faithfully reproduced is noise. Additional adjustable parameters let a model accommodate the accidents of a particular sample, and the price of that accommodation is paid when the model meets new data. Seen in this light, a preference for simplicity is a policy for estimating well from limited and imperfect evidence, not a belief about the architecture of the world. This answer has a cost that its admirers do not always acknowledge. If simplicity earns its keep by protecting against noise, then its value should shrink as data become more abundant and more precise, and statistical practice broadly bears this out: with enough clean data, more complex models often predict better, because they can capture real structure that a simple model would smooth away. Simplicity, on this account, is not a standing virtue but a discount applied in proportion to our ignorance. Nor is it clear that simplicity can even be measured independently of how a theory is written. Counting parameters seems objective until one notices that a relation expressed compactly in one set of variables may require several parameters when it is rewritten in another. None of this returns us to the view that simplicity is mere taste. The statistical argument shows that, in the situations scientists usually face, favouring the simpler of two well-fitting hypotheses is a reliable way to be less wrong. What it does not show is that the simpler hypothesis is, for that reason, more likely to be true; and the habit of speaking as though it did has lent the principle an authority it borrowed rather than earned.
R01-F-05: It is often said that a scientific theory can never be proved but can always be refuted: no number of successful predictions establishes it, while a single failed one brings it down. The slogan captures something real about the asymmetry between confirmation and refutation, but as a description of how theories should be treated it is too simple. A prediction is never derived from a theory alone. It depends also on assumptions about the instruments used, the conditions of the experiment and the other bodies or forces that might be at work. When a prediction fails, logic tells us that something in this whole bundle is wrong; it does not tell us which part. The history of astronomy offers a well-known illustration. In the first half of the nineteenth century, the observed orbit of Uranus departed from what Newtonian mechanics predicted. Astronomers did not abandon Newton. They supposed instead that an unseen planet was pulling on Uranus, calculated where it would have to be, and in 1846 Neptune was found close to the predicted position. The anomaly, far from refuting the theory, became one of its most celebrated successes. The same strategy, however, does not always succeed. A small discrepancy in the orbit of Mercury was also attributed to an undiscovered planet, which some astronomers even named, but no such planet was ever found. The discrepancy was finally accounted for only by Einstein's general theory of relativity, which replaced Newton's account of gravitation rather than adding to it. In hindsight, the two anomalies look entirely different. At the time, they looked much the same, and the decision to treat both in the same way was reasonable. The lesson is not that anomalies should be ignored, nor that theories should be given up at the first sign of trouble. It is that there is no rule which tells us in advance when an anomaly is a puzzle to be solved within a theory and when it is a sign that the theory is failing. Tenacity is a virtue in science, since a theory abandoned at the first difficulty would never have the chance to show what it can do; but tenacity shades into dogma when a theory is protected by one convenient assumption after another, each invented for no reason except to save it. Telling the two apart is a matter of judgement, informed by how many anomalies have accumulated and by whether the assumptions used to explain them away have earned independent support.
R01-F-06: A familiar picture of scientific objectivity confines values to the edges of inquiry. Values may legitimately decide which problems are worth studying and how results are used, but in the central act of science, deciding whether the evidence supports a hypothesis, they are supposed to have no place. A researcher who lets personal hopes affect whether a conclusion is accepted is, on this picture, simply doing bad science, and the remedy is a stricter separation between the laboratory and the world outside it. The trouble is that evidence rarely settles a question outright, and so accepting a hypothesis always involves deciding that the evidence is strong enough. How strong is strong enough? Consider a laboratory testing whether an industrial solvent damages the liver. If it wrongly concludes that the solvent is safe, workers may be harmed; if it wrongly concludes that the solvent is dangerous, a useful product may be withdrawn and money wasted. Which error is worse, and therefore how much evidence to demand before declaring the solvent harmful, is not something the data can decide. It depends on how one weighs injured workers against lost revenue, which is a question of value. Two laboratories examining identical data could therefore set the threshold in different places, and neither would have misread a single measurement. A natural reply is that scientists need not accept or reject anything. They could report the probability that the hypothesis is true, given the evidence, and leave the decision to those who must act. The reply is attractive but harder to carry out than it sounds. Before any probability can be reported, the investigators must decide how to classify ambiguous tissue samples, which measurements to discard as faulty and which statistical model to fit, and each of these decisions can err in either direction, with the same uneven consequences. The weighing of errors does not disappear; it moves to a stage where it is less visible. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that anything goes. The argument shows that values can properly bear on how much evidence to require, given what is at stake if one is wrong. It does not show that values can bear on what the evidence is, or license a researcher to discount an inconvenient result because it is unwelcome. The distinction is between setting the bar and moving the evidence, and the integrity of science depends on keeping the two apart, not on pretending that the bar sets itself.
R01-F-07: Thought experiments occupy an awkward place in the theory of knowledge. Scientists and philosophers have long used them to settle questions, and some of the most admired episodes in the history of physics turn on an imagined scenario rather than an actual measurement. Yet a thought experiment, by definition, collects no new data. The experimenter sits still and imagines. If we learn something about the world this way, it is not obvious where the information comes from, and two answers have dominated discussion. According to the first, a thought experiment is an argument in disguise. Its vivid scenario can always be rewritten as a set of premises and a conclusion, and whatever it teaches, it teaches because the premises were already believed and the conclusion follows from them. The imagery is persuasive packaging, useful perhaps for teaching, but adding nothing to the logical content. According to the second, the best thought experiments give us something no argument could: a kind of direct intellectual insight into the necessary structure of nature, as if the mind could see a law of physics in the way the eye sees a colour. Neither answer fits the most celebrated example well. Galileo asked his readers to imagine a heavy body and a light one tied together and dropped. If heavier bodies fall faster, as the received physics of his day held, the light body should hold back the heavy one, so that the pair falls more slowly than the heavy body alone; but the pair is heavier than the heavy body, so it should fall faster. The supposition contradicts itself, and the natural way out is that all bodies fall at the same rate, at least in the absence of a resisting medium. The argument reading can reconstruct this, but only by writing in premises that no one had formulated before the scenario was imagined: for instance, that the speed of a composite body must lie somewhere between the speeds of its parts. The insight reading, for its part, makes the result mysterious, as though Galileo had glimpsed a law rather than noticed a contradiction in what he and his readers already believed. A better account is that thought experiments work by drawing on knowledge we have but have never made explicit. Everyone who has carried a load or watched things fall has a large stock of tacit expectations about how bodies behave. A well-constructed scenario brings these expectations to bear on a case where they collide with an explicit theory, and so exposes a tension that was there all along. What is new is not the information but its arrangement. This explains why thought experiments can be genuinely informative without new data, and also why they cannot be reduced to an argument that someone might have written down beforehand: the premises are found by running the scenario, not before it. It also explains when they should not be trusted. Our tacit expectations were formed in a narrow band of experience, among objects of moderate size moving at moderate speeds. A thought experiment that asks us to imagine the very small, the very fast or the very distant invites us to apply those expectations where they were never tested, and the resulting conviction, however vivid, carries only the authority of the experience behind it. The method is neither a trick of rhetoric nor a window onto necessity. It is a way of interrogating what we already know, and it is exactly as reliable as that knowledge.
R01-F-08: Statements of chance are among the most familiar in science and ordinary life, and among the hardest to interpret. When we say that a fair coin has a chance of one half of landing heads, what are we saying? The most influential answer identifies chance with frequency: the chance of heads is the proportion of heads in a long run of tosses, or the limit towards which that proportion tends as the run is extended without end. The answer has the great merit of tying chance to something that can be counted, and it explains why observed frequencies are our main evidence about chances. Its difficulties begin with the single case. A particular coin may be tossed once and then melted down; a particular patient either will or will not recover from a particular operation. Yet we speak readily of the chance that this toss lands heads or that this patient recovers, and such judgements guide real decisions. The frequency view can treat them only by placing the single case in a class of similar cases and borrowing the frequency of the class. And here a second difficulty appears, because every case belongs to many classes. The patient is a man of sixty, a non-smoker, a resident of a particular city, someone treated by a particular surgeon, and the recovery rates in these classes may differ considerably. Which frequency is the patient's chance? Dissatisfaction with this reference class problem has led many to prefer a propensity view, on which chance is a physical tendency of a particular set-up to produce a given outcome, a property the single toss or the single operation possesses whether or not any long run ever occurs. The propensity view handles the single case gracefully, but at a price. It is unclear what a propensity is, beyond a name for whatever it is that frequencies are evidence of, and the view does not escape the problem it was meant to solve. The tendency of a set-up depends on how the set-up is described: the toss described as a toss of a fair coin has one propensity, while the toss described down to the exact force and angle of the flick may have another, close to certainty. The persistence of the problem across both views suggests that it is not a defect peculiar to either but a feature of chance itself. A chance is not a property an event has simply, but a property it has relative to a specification of the circumstances. Asking for the chance of an event, full stop, is like asking for the speed of a train without saying relative to what: the question is not unanswerable but incomplete. What remains open, and must be settled by our purposes rather than by the world, is which specification to use. For a gambler who cannot measure the flick, the description 'fair coin' is the relevant one; for a physicist with a high-speed camera, it is not. Some will feel that this concedes too much, making chance a matter of perspective rather than a feature of the world. But relativity to a description is not the same as subjectivity. Once the specification is fixed, the chance is fixed too, and two observers who adopt the same description and disagree about the chance cannot both be right. Velocity is no less objective for being relative to a frame. What the account gives up is only the idea that there is a single privileged description, the one nature itself would choose, and it is far from clear that anything in science requires such a description.
